title: Peter the Great and the Window to Europe

cards.b:
Peter the Great ruled Russia from 1682 and alone from 1696 to 1725. He wanted Russia to be a European power. He fought wars, built a new capital, and changed the way Russia was governed, taxed and educated.

Peter's reign set the pattern of Russian history for centuries. Historians still argue about whether he modernised Russia or merely copied the West.

cards.h: A young tsar and a palace revolt
cards.b:
Peter was born in 1672. He became joint tsar at ten with his half-brother Ivan, after a palace uprising. His half-sister Sophia ruled as regent until a new revolt in 1689 forced her out.

As a youth, Peter was fascinated by ships, foreign engineering and military drill. He built a small fleet on Lake Pleshcheyevo and a set of model soldiers, and he learned the basics of shipbuilding.

In 1697 Peter travelled through Europe with a large embassy. He went incognito under the name Peter Mikhailov, and he worked in the Dutch shipyards and the English dockyards. He also visited Prussia.

The trip brought back new ideas about ships, medicine, printing and government. Peter also brought foreign craftsmen and officers to Russia, and he began to push his nobles to adopt Western dress and manners.

Table of Ranks

Peter's Table of Ranks set out 14 grades for civil and military service. Anyone who reached a certain grade gained noble status, whatever his birth. Service to the state became the path to power.

The reform was a major break with older ideas of birth and privilege, though nobles still kept most of their advantages.
Peter's reign combined war, reform and building. It turned Russia into a major European state.

In 1700 Russia joined a coalition against Sweden. The war lasted until 1721. At first the Swedes won, but at Poltava in 1709 Peter's army defeated Charles XII. The victory gave Russia control of the Baltic coast.

Peter's army was trained on European lines, with a new officer corps and better artillery. The war cost Russia huge sums, and it was paid for with taxes, conscription and forced labour.

cards.h: St Petersburg: a window to Europe
cards.b:
In 1703 Peter founded St Petersburg on the marshy delta of the Neva river. Thousands of serfs died building it. The city became the new capital in 1712 and a model of European planning, with canals, palaces and straight avenues.

Peter called it his "window to Europe". The city was a bold symbol of change, and historians still debate whether the price was worth paying.

cards.h: Did Peter personally cut off beards?
cards.b:
A popular image shows Peter the Great with scissors, cutting the beards of his nobles. The picture is vivid and easy to remember.

Peter did impose a beard tax and ordered nobles to shave, and many men resisted. Historians argue about how far Peter personally enforced these rules. The beard tax was real, but the image of Peter as a single barber is exaggerated.

Historians argue about what Peter's reforms meant. Some say he modernised Russia by making its army, navy, administration and science more effective. Others say he westernised a society that was not ready, and that the reforms created a split between elites and peasants.

The debate is still alive, because Russians still argue about how Russia should relate to Europe. Peter remains a central figure in that argument.

cards.h: A tsar who was also a worker
cards.b:
Peter took a practical interest in trades. He learned carpentry and shipbuilding, and he worked as a shipwright in the Netherlands. He was very tall, around two metres, and he had a fierce temper.

His personal energy made him a figure of legend. He also drove his subjects hard, and many did not share his enthusiasm for change.

When Peter founded St Petersburg in 1703, the Mughal empire was still ruling India under Aurangzeb, who died in 1707. The decades after his death brought revolts by Marathas, Sikhs and regional governors.

In 1739 Nadir Shah of Persia sacked Delhi and took the Peacock Throne. Russia was rising, and India was splitting into rival states. The two empires faced very different futures.

Five things to remember
  1. Peter ruled alone from 1696.
  2. His Great Embassy to Europe ran from 1697 to 1698.
  3. He founded St Petersburg in 1703.
  4. The Table of Ranks of 1722 linked noble status to state service.
  5. Russia became an empire in 1721.
Think about it
  • Can a state modernise without copying others?
  • Was St Petersburg worth the human cost of building it?
